comments.author: @dawidm6893
comments.text: This test reminds me a bit of the stories I generate using AI. 100-200k tokens of contextual information about characters (extremely detailed, even what gestures someone makes and what they like for breakfast), the world, culture, laws, etc. Then I throw these characters into a specific point in history. Unfortunately, AI still has a unique problem with this. Since there are even 200k tokens of contextual information, I mainly test Gemini. It's weak, but with potential for the future. For example, the Gemini-1.5-pro version had 0/100 ability according to my criteria, Gemini-2.0-pro was around 1/100, while Gemini-2.5-pro is already about 5/100. It can utilize skills, talents, and even items possessed by a given person. The model naturally builds teams, as well as hostilities between characters. The biggest problem is that it has no planning for what will happen in 100-200k tokens, so the entire story is exceptionally weak. Maybe models in 3 years will be able to do something truly surprising, even wow-worthy.

comments.author: @hiper2d
comments.text:
I'm also developing a Werewolf game with AI. In my case, I participate it as a player. My model selection is wider: I have OpenAI models, Anthropic models, Grok, DeepSeek, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Kimi 2, Mistral. I don't see that much of deceptive behavior by default. They all are super friendly and logical, don't want to vote or make guesses without collecting facts. They all usually team up against me because my role-play is different. I had to prompt randomized personalities with different play styles to make the game actually interesting. Some bots are agressive, some bots are protective, some bots change sides, etc. And even then, in a long conversation, they tend to deviate from their system prompts and fall back to their default behavior. Some models like Gemini 2.5 Flash or Claude 3.5 Haiku are not good enough and can reveal their roles accidently, I had to exclude them.

Overall, a lot depends on prompting. Simply throwing some models to a game and let them play is not good enough. At least, my experience is poor. They don't play like humans, they don't use strategies which make a game fun or interesting. Things get better with manual personalities and play styles tunning. Summarizations help bots to develop ideas and plans. I let wolfs to talk a bit during the night, and they are very good in planning evil stuff. Grok-4, Opus 4.1, GPT-5 are probably the best in combining role-play with strategic thinking. Kimi sometimes replies in Chinese. Mistral Large is too straightforward and boring, DeepSeek is super slow, Gemini 2.5 Pro sometimes forgets its character name. But yeah, it's a fun way to test models. Every time a new model is in town, I add it to the game and let it play. It's a good benchmark for a model logic.

comments.author: @fetfree
comments.text:
Here's a benchmark-game for LLM.
0123456789. To go from 0 to 9, you need 9 jumps. From 0 to 1, one jump. From 1 to 2, another jump, etc. in a row. 
Unless you found out the algorithms linking those string of numbers. 2 by 2
Meaning finding the 5 pairs of numbers linked by an algorithm allowing you to skip jumps.
Example and hint:
69. The obvious one. The algorithm being vertical rotation, Inversion. Therefore if you know that algorithm and reached 6, then you can skip jump 7 and jump 8. 
From 6 straight to 9 in one jump.

That said I asked an AI to find the 5 pairs and their respective algorithms, given the hint above to get from 0 to 9 in 3 jumps. It couldn't while it found 4 out of 5 pairs. It could make it in 4 jumps instead of 9.
That's beyond human...in that specific case.
